transcription.tex: \textbf{Displacement–time graphs}\par Describe each graph: a horizontal line; a rising straight line; a rising curve whose gradient increases.
Horizontal: stationary.\par Rising straight line: constant positive velocity.\par Increasing positive gradient: positive acceleration.

\textbf{Velocity is the gradient}\[v=\frac{ds}{dt}\] \[\text{Average velocity}=\frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}\] \[\text{Average speed}=\frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}}\] Returning to the starting point gives zero overall displacement, even when the distance travelled is not zero.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A cyclist rides in a straight line for 20 minutes. She waits for half an hour, then returns in a straight line to her starting point in 15 minutes. This is a displacement-time graph for her journey.\par (a) Work out the average velocity for each stage of the journey in \(\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).\par (b) Write down the average velocity for the whole journey.\par (c) Work out average speed for the whole journey.
Overall displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero.\[\text{Average speed}=\frac{10}{65/60}=9.23\text{ km/h}.\]

transcription.tex: 2. Khalid drives from his home to a hotel. He drives for 2½ hours at an average velocity of 60 km/h. He then stops for lunch before continuing to his hotel. The diagram shows a displacement–time graph for Khalid's journey. \par (a) Work out the displacement of the hotel from Khalid's home. \par (b) Work out Khalid's average velocity for his whole journey.\par Problem-solving: Use the first stage of the journey to work out the vertical scale on the graph.
First stage: \(60\times2.5=150\) km. Each square represents \(150/6=25\) km.\[s=7.5\times25=187.5\text{ km}.\]

transcription.tex: 3. Sarah left home at 10:00 and cycled north in a straight line. The diagram shows a displacement–time graph for her journey. \par (a) Work out Sarah's velocity between 10:00 and 11:00. On her return journey, Sarah continued past her home before returning. \par (b) Estimate the time that Sarah passed her home. \par (c) Work out Sarah's velocity for each of the last two stages of her journey. \par (d) Calculate Sarah's average speed for her entire journey.
\[v=12/1=12\text{ km/h north}.\]
The return velocity is \(-10\) km/h, so 12 km takes 1.2 hours. She passes home at about 12:42 (approximately 12:45 from the sketch).
\[v_3=\frac{-3-12}{1.5}=-10\text{ km/h}\]\[v_4=3\text{ km/h}.\] \[\text{Average speed}=30/4=7.5\text{ km/h}.\]

transcription.tex: 4. A ball is thrown vertically up in the air and falls to the ground. This is a displacement–time graph for the motion of the ball. \par (a) Find the maximum height of the ball and the time at which it reaches that height. \par (b) Write down the velocity of the ball when it reaches its highest point. \par (c) Describe the motion of the ball: (i) from the time it is thrown to the time it reaches its highest point (ii) after reaching its highest point.
Maximum height: 2.5 m at 0.75 s. At the highest point, the graph has zero gradient, so velocity is \(0\text{ m/s}\).

Before the highest point, velocity is positive and decreases to zero. Afterwards velocity is negative and becomes more negative: the ball speeds up downwards. With no air resistance, it returns to the launch height with the same speed as at launch.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Velocity–time graphs}\par A line on the time axis means stationary. A horizontal line above the axis means constant positive velocity. A rising straight line means constant positive acceleration.

\textbf{Gradient and area}\[a=\frac{dv}{dt}\] Signed area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.\par To find total distance, add the magnitudes of areas above and below the time axis.\par Area under a speed–time graph gives distance. These coincide only when the velocity does not change sign.

transcription.tex: A cyclist travels at 6 m/s for 8 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest over 4 s. Find her displacement and deceleration.
\[s=6\times8+\tfrac12\times4\times6=60\text{ m}.\]
\[a=\frac{0-6}{4}=-1.5\text{ m/s}^2.\] Deceleration is \(1.5\text{ m/s}^2\).

transcription.tex: A particle moves along a straight line. The particle accelerates uniformly from rest to a velocity of 8 ms-1 in \(T\) seconds. The particle then travels at a constant velocity of 8 ms-1 for \(5T\) seconds. The particle then decelerates uniformly to rest in a further 40 s.\par (a) Sketch a velocity-time graph to illustrate the motion of the particle.\par Give then the total displacement of the particle is 600m.\par (b) find the value of \(T\).
Join \((0,0),(T,8),(6T,8),(6T+40,0)\) with straight lines. The middle section is horizontal.
\[\tfrac12(8)T+8(5T)+\tfrac12(8)(40)=600\] \[44T+160=600\quad\Rightarrow\quad T=10\text{ s}.\]

transcription.tex: A car is travelling along a straight horizontal road. The car takes 120 s to travel between two sets of traffic lights which are 2145 m apart. The car starts from rest at the first set of traffic lights and moves with constant acceleration for 30 s until its speed is 22 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The car maintains this speed for T seconds. The car then moves with constant deceleration, coming to rest at the second set of traffic lights. \par (a) Sketch, in the space below, a speed–time graph for the motion of the car between the two sets of traffic lights. (2) \par (b) Find the value of T. (3) A motorcycle leaves the first set of traffic lights 10 s after the car has left the first set of traffic lights. The motorcycle moves from rest with constant acceleration, a \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and passes the car at the point A which is 990 m from the first set of traffic lights. When the motorcycle passes the car, the car is moving with speed 22 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). \par (c) Find the time it takes for the motorcycle to move from the first set of traffic lights to the point A. (4) \par (d) Find the value of a. (2)
The car travels \(\tfrac12(30)(22)=330\) m initially.\[t_{\rm car}=30+\frac{990-330}{22}=60\text{ s}.\] Motorcycle time \(=60-10=50\) s.
\[990=\tfrac12a(50)^2\Rightarrow a=0.792\text{ m/s}^2.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Constant-acceleration equations}\par \(s\): displacement; \(u\): initial velocity; \(v\): final velocity; \(a\): constant acceleration; \(t\): duration.\par Use a consistent positive direction and the same time interval for every quantity.
Derive two equations using the straight velocity–time graph.
Gradient: \[a=\frac{v-u}{t}\Rightarrow v=u+at.\] Signed trapezium area: \[s=\frac{u+v}{2}t.\]

She then decelerates from 5 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to rest with constant deceleration \(\tfrac12 x\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find: \par (a) the value of x \par (b) the total distance she travelled.
Deceleration \(=0.125\text{ m/s}^2\), so stopping time \(=5/0.125=40\) s.\[d=\tfrac12(5)(20)+\tfrac12(5)(40)=150\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: 13. A particle is moving with constant acceleration in a straight line. It passes through three points A, B and C, with velocities 20 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), 30 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and 45 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. The time taken to move from A to B is \(t_1\) seconds and the time taken to move from B to C is \(t_2\) seconds. \par (a) Show that \(\frac{t_1}{t_2}=\frac23\). (3 marks) Given also that the total time taken for the particle to move from A to C is 50 s: \par (b) find the distance between A and B. (5 marks)
\[t_2=\tfrac32t_1\Rightarrow\tfrac52t_1=50\Rightarrow t_1=20.\] \[AB=\tfrac12(20+30)20=500\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Eliminate time}\[s=\frac{u+v}{2}\frac{v-u}{a}\]
\textbf{Eliminate final velocity}\[s=\frac{u+(u+at)}2t\]
\[s=ut+\tfrac12at^2.\]
\textbf{Eliminate initial velocity}\[s=\frac{(v-at)+v}{2}t\]
\[s=vt-\tfrac12at^2.\] All these equations require constant acceleration.

A particle is moving in a straight horizontal line with constant deceleration 4 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At time \(t=0\) the particle passes through a point \(O\) with speed 13 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) travelling towards a point \(A\), where \(OA=20\) m. transcription.tex: A lorry is moving along a straight horizontal road with constant acceleration. The lorry passes a point A with speed u \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), (u< 34), and 10 seconds later passes a point B with speed 34 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At time t = 0, P passes through the origin O with velocity 14 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in the positive direction. The point A lies on the axis and OA = 22.5 m. transcription.tex: \textbf{Vertical motion under gravity}\par Model the body as a particle and neglect air resistance. Near Earth, use \(g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2\), unless the question specifies another value.\par Acceleration is downward throughout the flight, including at the highest point.

\textbf{Choose a positive direction}\par Up positive: \(a=-g\). Down positive: \(a=+g\).\par At the highest point, \(v=0\); the acceleration is still downward.\par Keep unrounded values during calculation and round final answers as the question requests.\par The constant-acceleration equations apply separately to each uninterrupted stage.

transcription.tex: A book falls off the top shelf of a bookcase. The shelf is 1.4 m above a wooden floor. Find:\par (a) the time the book takes to reach the floor,\par (b) the speed with which the book strikes the floor.
Take downwards positive.\[1.4=\tfrac12(9.8)t^2\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{1.4/4.9}=0.535\text{ s}.\]
\[v^2=2(9.8)(1.4)\Rightarrow v=5.24\text{ m/s}.\] To 2 significant figures: 0.53 s and 5.2 m/s.

transcription.tex: A ball is projected vertically upwards, from a point \(X\) which is 7m above the ground, with speed 21 ms-1. Find\par (a) the greatest height above the ground reached by the ball,\par (b) the time of flight of the ball
At the highest point \(v=0\):\[0=21^2-2(9.8)s\Rightarrow s=22.5\text{ m}.\] Height above ground \(=22.5+7=29.5\) m.
At the ground, displacement from launch is \(-7\) m.\[-7=21t-4.9t^2\] The positive root is \(t=4.60\) s (3 s.f.).

11. A particle is projected vertically upwards from a point O with speed u \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Two seconds later it is still moving upwards and its speed is \(\frac13u\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). transcription.tex: 12. A ball A is thrown vertically downwards with speed 5 \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from the top of a tower block 46 m above the ground. \[s_A=5t+4.9t^2,\quad s_B=18t-4.9t^2\] \[s_A+s_B=46\Rightarrow23t=46\Rightarrow t=2\text{ s}.\]
\[s_A=5(2)+4.9(2)^2=29.6\text{ m}.\] This is measured downwards from the tower top.
